messages.subject: deer spotlight survey w/ double observer
parts:
Distance Sampling members,

I used distance sampling to estimate deer density in the Black Hills of S=
outh Dakota. We conducted spotlight surveys between 10 August to 21 Augus=
t 2009. Roads were selected to represent habitat in proportion seen throu=
ghout the study area. The survey route consisted of 43.9 km on 8 transect=
s that traveled through pine forest, meadows, aspen, and spruce. Deer we=
re counted on the same route 8 different nights. Two trucks ran 4 transec=
ts each night and switched routes every other night. We hypothesized that=
due to terrain and sapling regeneration along roads observers from the b=
ack of the vehicle would detect more animals because of a better angle an=
d higher view. We used 4 observers with 2 positioned in the cab and 2 obs=
ervers in the back of the truck. The front was considered the primary ob=
server and the back counted any additional animals the front did not see.=
The observers switched roles at the beginning of each new transect to e=
nsure that sightability differences were caused by position in the vehicl=
e and not the observer. We assumed that sighting probabilities associate=
d with each observer did not change with their role as primary or seconda=
ry observer. An observer could signal that a deer had been seen, but the =
count of each deer group was not announced until the vehicle had passed t=
he deer group.=20

Only one distance was recorded for each group sighting, so basically I wa=
s looking at the difference in total counts between front and back of the=
truck.

I am struggling with how I should analyze this data in distance? Should =
I use a double-observer technique in the MCDS engine? Or do I have to us=
e MRDS. I am afraid that observer independence assumption would be violat=
ed if using the MRDS engine. I thought maybe another option would be to =
develop a correction factor for total count and add that as a multiplier =
in the CDS engine.

Any suggestions would be greatly appreciated.
Thanks for your time,

Angela Jarding
Graduate Research Assistant
South Dakota State University
Brookings, SD 57007
angela....@sdstate.edu

messages.author: 12f269733c6eb9a2
messages.subject: Re: deer spotlight survey w/ double observer
parts:
Angela:

The analysis of anyone's data ought to be driven by the design of the=20
data collection. In your situation, what was the motivation for having=20
two sets of observers if they were not operating independently, or=20
setting up trials for one another? Further, why would you place the=20
'primary' data gatherers in the least optimal viewing locations?

Were you trying to overcome failure to detect deer on the trackline (the =

g(0) problem); in which you use the independent observer method=20
accounting for duplicate detections. Did you fear there was responsive=20
movement on the part of the deer to your approach (in which case you=20
should have used the Buckland-Turnock configuration) where one observer=20
was setting up trials for the other observer (but this relies upon a=20
particular type of viewing behaviour on the part of the tracker (in the=20
back of the truck) and the ability to determine successes/failures of=20
observers in the cab).

If you were simply trying to get lots of eyeballs looking for deer, then =

you really were not employing a double observer protocol per se, such=20
that the MRDS analytical protocol does not apply.

Prof. Buckland would find me remiss if I did not also mention that your=20
use of roads results in non-random sampling of the area you are trying=20
to study, so your density estimates may well not be representative of=20
your study area, but rather the portion of your study area that is near=20
roads. Similarly, it is likely the case that deer are not distributed=20
uniformly between the trackline out to your truncation distance (there=20
is little for a deer to eat in the centre of a gravel road so deer are=20
unlikely to be there, if sapling regeneration is good all the road edges =

there are more likely to be there browsing). See the forthcoming paper=20
*Point Transect Sampling Along Linear Features, *T. A. Marques, S. T.=20
Buckland, D. L. Borchers, D. Tosh, R. A. McDonald DOI:=20
10.1111/j.1541-0420.2009.01381.x appearing soon in Biometrics for a=20
discussion of this non-uniform distribution issue.

So you have a handful of sampling issues you need to ponder beyond your=20
multiple observer matter.

messages.author: 5140016d70f6ba82
messages.subject: Re: deer spotlight survey w/ double observer
parts:
Eric covers some important points but missed the concept that you were
using the removal design which is easier to implement in the field and
eliminates the need to do matching after the fact. Rotating observers
will allow you to estimate observer differences but there cannot be any
differences due to position which it sounds like there may be in this
case, but hard for me to evaluate.

--jeff
